name: RoCEv2 PFC-based lossless Ethernet suffers incast collapse at GPU scale
symptom: RoCEv2 networks using PFC (Priority-based Flow Control) for lossless operation experience throughput collapse and latency spikes when GPU count exceeds a threshold, typically around 1000-2000 GPUs in a single network domain.
root_cause: PFC creates a lossless domain by pausing upstream switches when buffers fill. Under incast patterns (many-to-one traffic common in all-reduce collectives), PFC pause frames propagate upstream, creating head-of-line blocking and cascading congestion. DCQCN (Data Center Quantized Congestion Notification) provides ECN-based rate limiting but cannot fully prevent incast collapse at scale because the fundamental issue is many-to-one traffic patterns overwhelming a single destination port.
workaround: Use InfiniBand instead (hardware-based congestion control with per-credit flow control, no PFC). Or implement Ultra Ethernet (UEC) which redesigns the transport to avoid PFC. Or use rail-optimized network topology to reduce incast patterns. Or limit the number of GPUs per lossless domain.
notes: This is the primary reason InfiniBand dominates large-scale AI training clusters despite higher cost. The incast problem is fundamental to PFC-based lossless Ethernet and cannot be fully solved with tuning. NVIDIA's Spectrum-X platform claims to address this with advanced RoCE extensions and congestion management, but independent verification at scale is limited. The problem is well-documented in academic literature (e.g., 'Congestion Control for Large-Scale RDMA Deployments' by Zhu et al., SIGCOMM 2016).
